title: Constantly Searching for Meaning Could Cause Burnout
paragraphs: Having a sense of meaning in life is often seen as good for our well-being. But according to a new study, constantly searching for meaning may actually be linked to a higher risk of burnout at work.

The study was published in the Journal of Health Psychology by Rachel Sumner of the University of Bristol, Elaine Kinsella of the University of Limerick and Wijnand van Tilburg of the University of Essex. It used data from the CV19 Heroes Project, a long-term study of frontline workers in the UK and Ireland, most of whom work in health and social care.

The researchers first surveyed 1,239 people in March and April 2020, at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. They then followed up with them every year until 2023. The surveys measured two things: how much meaning people felt they had in their lives, and how much they were searching for meaning. They also measured burnout, including exhaustion, cynicism and feelings of not being good enough.

The results showed that people who had a stronger sense of meaning tended to experience less burnout. However, people who were searching for meaning tended to experience more burnout. The combination of having little meaning and searching hard for it seemed to be the worst. People in this situation reported the highest levels of cynicism and overall burnout.

Van Tilburg, who led the analysis, said that this combination of low meaning and high searching seemed particularly problematic. Kinsella added that meaning appears to be an important psychological resource for frontline workers.

However, the study has some important limitations that should be kept in mind. It shows a connection, not a cause. It is possible that people start searching for meaning because they are already beginning to feel burned out. In addition, many participants left the study over time, and most of those who took part were white women working in health care.
